finding.title: Gzip branch shadows err, so write and close errors are never returned

findings.title: Gzip branch shadows err, so write and close errors are never returned
findings.scenario: Run with -gzip while the write fails (for example, disk full). writeEntries returns an error into the inner err, which is discarded. The outer err stays nil, Write returns nil, main does not call os.Remove, and the log reports success. A partial .gz file is left behind, which is the outcome the author asked to prevent. The same happens when compressed.Close() fails, because it also assigns to the inner err.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No type or compiler check catches the shadowed := declaration. The diff adds no test for the gzip path or for a write error in that path, and go vet's default checks do not flag this shadowing.

finding.title: gzip path shadows err, so write and close errors are dropped

findings.title: gzip path shadows err, so write and close errors are dropped
findings.scenario: Run with -gzip when the disk fills mid-write. writeEntries fails inside the inner block, but the := declares a new err that is never returned. Write returns the outer nil, main skips its os.Remove branch, and a truncated .gz file is left behind. The same happens when compressed.Close() fails, because its error is also assigned to the inner err.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The outer `var err error` is still nil on this path, and nothing checks the return value of the gzip branch. No test covers -gzip with a failing writer.

findings.title: Gzip write errors are shadowed and dropped, so a failed export is reported as success and leaves a partial file
findings.scenario: Run with -gzip and the disk fills or the writer fails mid-write. writeEntries returns an error, but `:=` creates a new inner err. The `if err == nil` check and the Close call also use the inner variable. The function returns the outer err, which is still nil, so Write returns nil. main.go sees success, does not call os.Remove, and the truncated .gz file stays on disk.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The compiler accepts the shadowed variable, and go vet does not flag it by default. No test in the diff covers a failing writer on the gzip path, so nothing catches it.

other.title: Sum checksum misses reordered bytes and offsetting multi-byte errors
No write path in the repo calls encode, so records written to the journal get no checksum

findings.title: Sum checksum misses reordered bytes and offsetting multi-byte errors
findings.scenario: Two bytes swapped in a record, e.g. b"ab" stored as b"ba", keep the same sum and decode as valid. Two corruptions that offset each other mod 256 also pass.
findings.whyNotPrevented: A sum is order-independent and weak against compensating errors. The stated goal is single-byte corruption, which a sum does catch, so this is a limit of the design, not a failure of the requested behavior.

findings.title: No write path in the repo calls encode, so records written to the journal get no checksum
findings.scenario: A journal writer that appends bodies directly, without calling encode, produces records with no trailing checksum. Replay then reads the last body byte as the checksum and reports Corrupted for valid records.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Nothing in the diff or the tests connects encode to a writer. The only callers found are in record.rs tests, so this check cannot tell whether a writer exists elsewhere.

other.title: Sum checksum does not detect reordered bytes

findings.title: Sum checksum does not detect reordered bytes
findings.scenario: Swapping two bytes in a body, for example b"ab" to b"ba", leaves the sum unchanged, so decode returns Ok with the wrong body and replay applies it
findings.whyNotPrevented: The checksum is order-independent, and the tests only flip a single byte (a_flipped_byte_is_caught)

findings.title: Sum checksum misses reordered bytes
findings.scenario: body b"ab" and b"ba" have the same sum, so a record whose two bytes were swapped on disk still decodes as valid and replays wrong data
findings.whyNotPrevented: the sum is order-independent, and the tests only flip a single byte (a_flipped_byte_is_caught), so no test covers transposition

finding.title: Length truncated to u16 while the size limit allows up to 256 KiB

findings.title: Length truncated to u16 while the size limit allows up to 256 KiB
findings.scenario: A 70,000-byte message passes the MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES check (262,144 bytes), then the header is written as 70000 as u16 = 4464. The body of 70,000 bytes follows, so the decoder reads 4,464 bytes as one frame and treats the remaining bytes as the start of the next frame. The stream desyncs with no error. Any message over 65,535 bytes is affected.
findings.whyNotPrevented: encode only checks message.len() > MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES, and MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES is 256 * 1024 (src/limits.rs:2). Nothing checks the length against u16::MAX. The only test for the limit uses MAX + 1, and the new test uses a 5-byte message, so neither covers the 65,536 to 262,144 range.
findings.measuredBy: Grep "MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES" in repo: src/limits.rs:2 defines it as 256 * 1024; src/frame.rs:12 is the only check in encode

finding.title: Lengths above 65535 bytes are silently truncated by the u16 cast

findings.title: Lengths above 65535 bytes are silently truncated by the u16 cast
findings.scenario: A 65536-byte message passes the MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES check (256 * 1024 = 262144) and is encoded with length 0x0000. decode reads length 0, returns an empty message, and treats the 65536 payload bytes as the start of the next frame. Any message from 65536 to 262144 bytes is corrupted or desynchronizes the stream.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The only size check compares against MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES, which is 262144 in src/limits.rs, and nothing ties that limit to u16::MAX. The added test only encodes b"hello", and the existing TooLarge test only checks the 262145-byte boundary, so no test exercises 65536 or more bytes.
findings.measuredBy: Grep "MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES" in src: src/limits.rs:2 defines it as 256 * 1024; src/frame.rs:18 casts message.len() to u16 with no range check

finding.title: Messages over 65535 bytes get a truncated length header and corrupt the stream

findings.title: Messages over 65535 bytes get a truncated length header and corrupt the stream
findings.scenario: A 70,000-byte message passes the MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES check (256 KiB). The `as u16` cast writes a length of 4464 (70000 mod 65536), but all 70,000 bytes are appended. decode reads 4464 bytes as one message and treats the remaining 65,536 bytes as the start of the next frame, so the stream is misparsed with no error.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The only size check, at line 12, compares against MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES = 256 * 1024 (src/limits.rs:2), which is larger than u16::MAX. The new test uses b"hello" and the existing too-large test only covers MAX+1, so no test exercises lengths between 65536 and 262144.
findings.measuredBy: Grep "MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES" in repo: src/limits.rs:2 defines it as 256 * 1024; src/frame.rs:12 is the only size check before the u16 cast on line 18

finding.title: Late-binding lambda makes every field use the body limit of 5000

findings.title: Late-binding lambda makes every field use the body limit of 5000
findings.scenario: A title of 81 characters, which should fail the 80 limit, passes validate(). The lambdas read `limit` only when called, after the loop has finished, so every validator compares against 5000. The same happens to summary at 281 characters, which should fail the 280 limit and passes. validate({"title": "x" * 81}) returns [] instead of ["title is too long"].
findings.whyNotPrevented: The added test only checks body with 5001 characters. Nothing tests title or summary at their limits, and no type or lint check flags the closure over a loop variable.

findings.title: byClient map is never initialized, so the first Record call panics
findings.scenario: The server starts (main.go:13 calls stats.New), then the first request passes through Counted, which calls Record(clientOf(r), status). Record runs s.byClient[client]++ on a nil map, which panics with 'assignment to entry in nil map'. Every request fails before its count is recorded, so the summary never shows busiest clients.
findings.whyNotPrevented: New only makes byStatus. Grep for byClient finds only the field declaration, the increment in Record, and the read in Summary, with no make call. No test covers Record or New, so nothing catches the nil map.

findings.title: clientOf falls back to the raw RemoteAddr when SplitHostPort fails
findings.scenario: net/http always sets RemoteAddr to host:port for server requests, so the error branch is not reached in practice. If it were reached, the raw string would become the client key without any report of the failure.
findings.whyNotPrevented: net/http sets RemoteAddr itself, so the branch is a fallback for a state the change does not show can happen.

findings.title: Vents never open until five readings exist, even when the early readings are already hot
findings.scenario: readings [35.0, 35.0, 35.0, 35.0] (four readings, all far above 28.0): trailing_average returns an empty Vec, so should_open returns false and the vents stay closed. The old mean-based code returned true for the same input.
findings.whyNotPrevented: no caller or test in the repo covers should_open with fewer than five readings; the new test too_few_readings_give_nothing asserts the empty result but nothing checks what the vents should do in that state

findings.title: should_open has no test for the threshold or for the newest-reading case

findings.title: Vents never open on a hot start until five readings exist
findings.scenario: temperatures = [35.0] or [35.0, 35.0, 35.0, 35.0]: trailing_average returns an empty Vec because values.len() < 5, so should_open returns false. The old mean-based code returned true for both, so the vents now stay shut during the first four readings even when they are very hot.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The early return in src/readings.rs (line 10) converts 'fewer than five readings' into an empty result, and should_open treats an empty result as 'not hot'. No test calls should_open, and the new readings tests only cover trailing_average.

findings.scenario: A regression in should_open, such as using the first window instead of the last, or the short-input case above, would pass the current test suite.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The added tests in src/readings.rs exercise trailing_average only. Grep for 'should_open' in tests finds no test that calls it.

finding.title: Trailing window never includes the newest reading, and exactly `window` readings give no average

findings.title: Trailing window never includes the newest reading, and exactly `window` readings give no average
findings.scenario: should_open(&[20.0, 30.0, 30.0, 30.0, 30.0, 30.0]) computes windows only for end=5, which is values[0..5] = [20,30,30,30,30] with mean 28.0. That is not > 28.0, so the vents stay closed. The last five readings are all 30.0 and should open them. With exactly five readings, e.g. should_open(&[29.0; 5]), the range 5..5 is empty, so it returns false even though the average is 29.0.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The new tests only use steady readings ([21.5; 6]) or too-short input ([20.0, 21.0]), so they cannot tell which window is last. No test calls should_open at all.

finding.title: Mutable default list accumulates TEAM_INBOX across calls

findings.title: Mutable default list accumulates TEAM_INBOX across calls
findings.scenario: build_digest(["a"]) then build_digest(["b"]) in the same process: the default list is shared and append mutates it, so the second digest has recipients [TEAM_INBOX, TEAM_INBOX]. A third call gives three copies. Each digest then sends the team inbox duplicate mail, and the list keeps growing.
findings.whyNotPrevented: test_team_inbox_gets_the_digest only checks the first call, and test_subject_counts_updates calls build_digest with no recipients and checks only the subject. No test calls build_digest twice without recipients and checks recipients.

findings.title: build_digest mutates the caller's recipients list
findings.scenario: send_weekly passes project.watchers() directly. If watchers() returns a stored list, each run appends TEAM_INBOX to that project's own watcher list, so the list changes after every digest build.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No code copies the list before appending. I could not locate a definition of watchers() under src/, so whether it returns a stored list is unverified.

finding.title: Mutable default list shares recipients across calls and grows each time

findings.title: Mutable default list shares recipients across calls and grows each time
findings.scenario: build_digest(["a"]) is called twice with no recipients argument. The first digest gets [TEAM_INBOX]. The second call reuses the same default list, which now holds TEAM_INBOX, so it gets [TEAM_INBOX, TEAM_INBOX] and the team inbox is duplicated. Over a long run in send_weekly the default list keeps growing.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The new test passes an explicit list, and the existing test only checks a single first call. Nothing calls build_digest twice with the default, so the shared state is never exercised. The existing test passes only because it runs first.

findings.title: append mutates the caller's watcher list in place
findings.scenario: send_weekly passes project.watchers() as recipients. If watchers() returns a list stored on the project, each run appends TEAM_INBOX to that stored list, so the project's own watcher list changes and later reads of it include the team inbox.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The diff does not show watchers(), and a grep of the repo for its definition found no match, so this cannot be confirmed here. Nothing in the diff copies the list before appending.
